text: In the Money, Plainly handbook, investing means putting money where it may grow, accepting that it may also fall.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, budget means a plan for the money coming in and going out.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, income means money coming in.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, expense means money going out.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, emergency fund means money set aside for a surprise cost.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, interest means money paid for the use of money.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, savings account means a bank account that pays interest on money you keep there.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, deposit insurance means the federal guarantee on bank deposits, up to a limit.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, credit union means a bank owned by its members.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, credit means borrowing now and paying back later.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, debt means money owed.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, interest rate means the price of borrowing, or the pay for saving, as a percentage a year.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, APR means the yearly cost of credit, interest plus some fees.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, credit report means the record lenders read before they lend.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, compound interest means interest earned on earlier interest as well as on the deposit.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, simple interest means interest earned only on the original deposit.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, principal means the money you put in, before any growth.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, rate of return means how much an investment gained or lost, as a percentage.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, SEC means the US agency that oversees securities markets and investor education.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, stock means a piece of ownership in a company.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, bond means a loan to a company or government that pays interest.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, mutual fund means a pool of investors' money bought into many securities, priced once a day.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, security means a tradable financial asset such as a stock or bond.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, index means a list of securities that stands for a market or part of one.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, index fund means a fund that tries to match an index rather than beat it.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, ETF means a fund whose shares trade on an exchange through the day.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, prospectus means the document a fund must give investors, with its goals, risks and costs.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, NAV means a fund's assets minus its debts, per share.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, risk means the chance of losing money or earning less than expected.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, diversification means spreading money across investments so one loss hurts less.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, asset allocation means how money is divided among stocks, bonds and cash.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, fee means a charge for a service, taken from your money or your returns.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, expense ratio means a fund's yearly costs as a percentage of the money invested.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, 401(k) means a workplace retirement plan.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, IRA means a retirement account you open yourself.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, Roth means a retirement account paid into after tax, with qualified withdrawals untaxed.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, IRS means the US tax agency.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, crypto asset means a digital asset recorded on a blockchain.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, CFPB means the US agency that protects consumers of financial products.
In the Money, Plainly handbook, scam means a scheme to take money by deceit.

Money, Plainly, chapter 1 (Where your money goes), in short: A budget is a plan for the money coming in and the money going out over a set period, usually a month. Money coming in is income. Money going out is an expense. You pay your needs first, like rent and groceries, and then choose wants from what is left. Before you can plan, you track every expense for a whole month, because small spending adds up. The goal is a gap at the end of the month that you can save.

Money, Plainly, chapter 2 (A cushion for bad days), in short: An emergency cushion is money kept aside for surprise bills, like a car repair or a medical bill. Surprises are normal: in 2025, more than half of adults had one. Without a cushion, people borrow, pay late, or raid retirement money, and a small bill grows. A first goal of a few hundred dollars covers many common shocks. A bigger cushion covers months without pay. Keep it safe, easy to reach, and away from everyday spending, and refill it after you use it.

Money, Plainly, chapter 3 (Banks, credit unions and deposit insurance), in short: A bank or credit union holds your money and lends it out, and it pays you interest for the use of it. Checking accounts are for spending, savings accounts are for setting money aside. If an insured bank fails, deposit insurance pays you back, up to $250,000 per person, per bank, per ownership category. A credit union is owned by its members and has matching federal insurance. Investments bought at a bank are not deposits, so they are not covered.

Money, Plainly, chapter 4 (Credit, debt and your credit report), in short: Credit is borrowing now and paying later, and debt is what you owe. The interest rate is the price of borrowing. On a card it is quoted yearly as the APR, which folds in other charges. Many cards charge interest daily on your average balance. Pay in full by the due date and you usually pay none on purchases. Pay only the minimum and interest piles onto the balance for years. Lenders read your credit report and score to decide whether to lend, and at what rate.

Money, Plainly, chapter 5 (Compound growth and time), in short: Compound interest means you earn interest on your deposit and on the interest it already earned, so growth speeds up over time. Simple interest pays only on the original deposit, so it grows in a straight line. At an assumed five percent, a thousand dollars compounding for thirty years ends far ahead of simple interest. The rate matters, but time matters most, and steady saving beats waiting for the perfect moment. No return is guaranteed.

Money, Plainly, chapter 6 (Stocks, bonds and funds: what an index fund and an ETF are), in short: A stock is a slice of ownership in a company. A bond is money you lend to a business or a government, which pays you interest and pays you back. A mutual fund pools many people's money and buys many securities, and you buy and sell its shares through the fund at the next calculated NAV. An index fund just tries to match a list of securities instead of beating it. An ETF is a fund whose shares trade on an exchange all day, at market prices.

Money, Plainly, chapter 7 (Risk, diversification and fees), in short: Risk is the chance that an investment loses money or does worse than you expected, and higher possible returns usually come with more of it. You cannot remove risk, but you can spread it. Diversification means owning many different investments so one loss hurts less. Asset allocation means choosing how much goes into stocks, bonds and cash, based on your time and your tolerance for loss. Fees are the cost you always pay. A small yearly fee, compounded over decades, can take a large share of what you would have had.

Money, Plainly, chapter 8 (Accounts and taxes: 401(k), IRA and Roth), in short: A 401(k) is a retirement plan through your job, and an IRA is one you open yourself. The big difference between account types is when you pay tax. Traditional accounts let you skip tax on the money going in, then tax the withdrawals in retirement. Roth accounts take after-tax money and let qualified withdrawals come out tax-free. Each account has a yearly limit set by the IRS, and the IRA limit is far smaller than the 401(k) limit.

Money, Plainly, chapter 10 (Scams and red flags), in short: A scam is a scheme to take money by deceit, and most scams leave the same marks. They promise high returns with no risk, which no real investment can do. They rush you, so you cannot check. They point to the crowd, buy you lunch, or wear a trusted name. They want gift cards, wires or crypto, and they charge a fee before you get anything. So I slow down, call the real number myself, look up the seller's license, get everything in writing, and walk away when it feels wrong.

Money, Plainly, chapter 11 (The first $1,000, walked through), in short: A first sum of savings follows an order. Pay off high interest debt first, because no investment can guarantee returns that outweigh a credit card's rate. Next, build an emergency fund in a separate savings account, filled by automatic transfers. Then invest regularly, starting with a workplace plan if there is a match, and an IRA after. Inside those accounts, choose a diversified, low-cost fund and read its prospectus. Before trusting anyone with the money, look them up and ignore promises of high returns with no risk.
